artworks.title: Mark Dion: Eccentric Collectors Like Us
artworks.description: The artist Mark Dion turns the special-exhibition gallery into a cabinet of curiosities inspired by Cummings E. Davis, the eccentric Concord collector whose objects started the museum: quirky portraits and engravings, weathervanes, a barber’s sign and dozens of objects rarely or never shown before. Instead of labels you get a Field Guide, and a hands-on installation invites you into the work of collecting.
artworks.galleryName: Special Exhibit Gallery (Wallace Kane Gallery)
artworks.placeNote: In this gallery, as the museum’s own floor plan names it.
artworks.imageCredit: Concord Museum

artworks.title: Family Trees: A Celebration of Children’s Literature
artworks.description: Opens Nov 21, 2026. Dozens of story trees decorated by local volunteers, each bringing a picture book to life, with a scavenger hunt and books to read together. The trees fill the museum; where exactly they stand is not on the map. Special ticket prices apply while it is on, and the museum also opens on Mondays in December.
artworks.galleryName: Brooke Hall
artworks.placeNote: Family Trees fills the museum; it is shown here in Brooke Hall, by the entrance.
artworks.imageCredit: Concord Museum

artworks.title: Chemacheg Menuhki: Paddle Strong
artworks.description: Regional Indigenous history and contemporary textile arts, with a fibre basket woven by Walley: a celebration of the continued presence and resilience of Indigenous communities today.
artworks.galleryName: People of Musketaquid: Indigenous history and art
artworks.placeNote: In this gallery, as the museum’s own floor plan names it.
artworks.imageCredit: Concord Museum

artworks.title: Musketaquid Gallery
artworks.description: The history and contemporary art of the Indigenous communities who have shaped this region for 12,000 years. Its centrepiece is a glass wall of 600 stone tools arranged in a Native design.
artworks.galleryName: People of Musketaquid: Indigenous history and art
artworks.placeNote: In this gallery, as the museum’s own floor plan names it.
artworks.imageCredit: Concord Museum

artworks.title: Concord: At the Center of Revolution
artworks.description: Fourteen iconic objects that give a first “brush” with Concord’s history, from Louisa May Alcott’s Civil War tea kettle to Abner Hosmer’s powder horn: the place to start your visit.
artworks.galleryName: Concord: At the Center of Revolution (introductory gallery)
artworks.placeNote: In this gallery, as the museum’s own floor plan names it.

artworks.title: Celebrated Transcendentalist Authors
artworks.description: The world of Concord’s writers: the Alcotts, Hawthorne, Emerson and Thoreau, their friendships, their social world and their political activism.
artworks.galleryName: Celebrated Transcendentalist Authors
artworks.placeNote: In this gallery, as the museum’s own floor plan names it.
artworks.imageCredit: Concord Museum

artworks.title: Thoreau’s desk
artworks.description: The plain green desk Thoreau used at Walden Pond, where he wrote much of Walden and A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers. Stand in front of it for a media presentation drawn from his own words. The museum has the world’s largest collection of Thoreau’s belongings.
artworks.galleryName: Thoreau’s Desk
artworks.placeNote: In this gallery, as the museum’s own floor plan names it.
artworks.imageCredit: photo by Daderot (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons

artworks.title: April 19, 1775
artworks.description: Three galleries on the day the American Revolution began, hour by hour, with dozens of objects that witnessed it, starting with the lantern from Paul Revere’s ride.

artworks.placeNote: In this gallery, as the museum’s own floor plan names it.
artworks.imageCredit: Concord Museum
